questions.hint: A prism has two identical parallel polygon ends and flat rectangular sides (all faces are flat). A cylinder has two flat circular ends and one curved wall.

keyPoints.text: all the prisms
keyPoints.note: Prisms have only flat faces: two identical parallel polygon bases and rectangular side faces.

keyPoints.text: all the cylinders
keyPoints.note: Cylinders have two flat circular ends connected by one curved surface.

questions.solution: The \(7\) prisms (coloured blue) are the Fruit Juice carton, Toy Box, Die (cube), Drawer tray, Tent, Triangular prism block, and Matchbox. The \(4\) cylinders (ticked) are the Jam tin, Birthday cake, Toilet paper roll, and Tall plain cylinder. The Cricket ball (sphere), Hexagonal pyramid, and Ice-cream cone are left unmarked.

steps.explain: Recall the difference between a prism and a cylinder: a prism has two identical polygon bases and flat rectangular sides (like the Fruit Juice carton in blue), while a cylinder has two circular ends and a curved wall (like the Jam tin in yellow).
steps.work: \(\text{Prism: flat polygon faces only},\quad \text{Cylinder: } 2\text{ circular ends} + 1\text{ curved surface}\)

keyPoints.text: classroom objects into prisms and cylinders
keyPoints.note: Books and tissue boxes have 6 flat rectangular faces (prisms); glue sticks and round pencil tins have 2 circular ends and a curved surface (cylinders).

questions.solution: A hardcover book and a tissue box are rectangular prisms (6 flat rectangular faces), while a glue stick and a round pencil tin are cylinders (2 flat circular ends and 1 curved surface).

questions.solution: The pentagonal prism (5th object from the top) has 2 pentagonal (5-sided) end faces and 5 rectangular side faces (\(2 + 5 = 7\) faces in total), which matches Row 2: 2 pentagons and 5 rectangles.

keyPoints.text: matches the 6th (bottom) 3D object on the left
keyPoints.note: Check the shape of the two parallel end faces and count the side faces on the 6th (bottom) 3D object on the left, then count down the rows on the right from Row 1 to Row 6.

questions.solution: The cylinder (bottom object) has 2 circular end faces and 1 curved surface that unrolls into a rectangle (\(2 + 1 = 3\) faces in total), which matches Row 6: 2 circles and 1 curved rectangular surface.

questions.hint: A face is a flat (or curved) surface, an edge is a line where two faces meet, and a corner is a point where edges meet.

keyPoints.text: words face, corner or edge to correctly label each set of arrows
keyPoints.note: A corner is a point where lines meet; an edge is a straight or curved line where two faces meet; a face is a surface.

questions.solution: In b, the arrows from top to bottom point to: Arrow 1: corner, Arrow 2: face, Arrow 3: corner.

steps.explain: Look at Arrow 1 at the top: it points directly to a vertex where three edges meet at a point, which is a corner.

meta.question: 7a

questions.stem: Identify the faces, edges and corners of the triangular pyramid shown. In b, if you trace over all the edges of the triangular pyramid (including the dashed hidden back edge), how many edges are there in total?

questions.hint: Count the \(3\) edges around the bottom triangular base and the \(3\) sloped edges going up to the top apex.

keyPoints.text: all the edges of the triangular pyramid
keyPoints.note: Count the base edges around the bottom triangle and the sloped edges meeting at the top point.

questions.solution: A triangular pyramid has \(3\) base edges and \(3\) sloped edges meeting at the apex, giving \(3 + 3 = 6\) edges in total.

steps.explain: Recall that an edge is a straight line segment where two flat faces meet.

questions.hint: Count the number of sides on the base of pyramid c, then remember that a pyramid has \(1\) base and a triangle for each side of that base.

keyPoints.text: Pyramids only have \(1\) base and all other faces are triangular
keyPoints.note: Count the edges of the base polygon on the left to know the base shape and how many triangular side faces meet at the apex.

questions.solution: The pyramid in c has a \(6\)-sided (hexagon) base and \(6\) triangular side faces, so its faces are \(1\) hexagon and \(6\) triangles.

questions.stem: Which description accurately describes the features of the RAZZ iceblock pyramid shown in Question 9?

options: It is a triangular pyramid with \(4\) triangular faces, \(6\) straight edges and \(4\) corners.
It is a square pyramid with \(1\) square base, \(4\) triangular faces, \(8\) edges and \(5\) corners.
It is a triangular prism with \(2\) triangular bases, \(3\) rectangular faces, \(9\) edges and \(6\) corners.
It is a cone with \(1\) circular flat base, \(1\) curved surface and \(1\) apex.
questions.hint: Count the faces, edges and corners of a pyramid that has a triangle as its base.

keyPoints.text: description accurately describes the features of the RAZZ iceblock pyramid
keyPoints.note: The RAZZ iceblock packet is a triangular pyramid (tetrahedron): 1 triangular base + 3 triangular sides = 4 faces, 6 edges, and 4 corners.

questions.solution: The RAZZ iceblock packet is a triangular pyramid with \(4\) triangular faces, \(6\) straight edges, and \(4\) corners.

steps.explain: Identify the base shape of the RAZZ iceblock pyramid: its base has \(3\) sides (a triangle), so it is a triangular pyramid.

options: All three containers have the same capacity
questions.hint: The smaller the container is, the more times you have to pour it to fill the same bowl. Find the container that needed the greatest number of pours.

keyPoints.text: smallest capacity
keyPoints.note: A smaller container holds less liquid per pour, so it takes more pours (the largest tally count) to fill the same bowl.

questions.solution: The tea cup needed \(9\) pours (compared to \(6\) mugs and \(5\) glasses) to fill the same bowl, so the tea cup has the smallest capacity.

steps.explain: Count the tally marks for each vessel in the table (highlighted in yellow): Mug \(= 6\), Tea cup \(= 9\), and Glass \(= 5\).

questions.hint: Count the tally marks in each row of the table (remember a crossed bundle equals \(5\)) and match each count to its column.

keyPoints.text: Mug, the Tea cup and the Glass from left to right
keyPoints.note: Each crossed tally bundle represents 5, and each single vertical stroke adds 1.

questions.solution: Counting the tallies gives Mug \(= 5 + 1 = 6\), Tea cup \(= 5 + 4 = 9\), and Glass \(= 5\).

steps.explain: Count the tally marks for Mug: \(1\) bundle of \(5\) plus \(1\) stroke equals \(6\).

questions.solution: A household kettle holds a few cups of water (around 1.5 L to 2 L), so a tea cup is the most suitable informal unit to measure it.

keyPoints.text: measuring the capacity of the fruit juice cask (4 L)
keyPoints.note: Match small containers to small vessels, medium containers to medium vessels, and large buckets to the 300 L bath.

meta.question: 10d

questions.stem: Record containers that have their capacity labelled: a Medicine bottle (\(100\text{ mL}\)), a Chocolate milk carton (\(250\text{ mL}\)), a Milk carton (\(1\text{ L}\)), a Cordial bottle (\(2\text{ L}\)), and a Fruit juice cask (\(4\text{ L}\)). Which list orders these capacities from smallest to largest?
questions.hint: Remember that millilitres (\(\text{mL}\)) are much smaller than litres (\(1\text{ L} = 1000\text{ mL}\)), so list the millilitre containers before the litre containers.

keyPoints.text: orders these capacities from smallest to largest
keyPoints.note: 1 L equals 1000 mL, so 100 mL and 250 mL are both smaller than 1 L.

questions.solution: Since \(1\text{ L} = 1000\text{ mL}\), the capacities in order from smallest to largest are \(100\text{ mL}, 250\text{ mL}, 1\text{ L}, 2\text{ L}, 4\text{ L}\).

steps.explain: Compare millilitres (\(\text{mL}\)) and litres (\(\text{L}\)): \(1\text{ L} = 1000\text{ mL}\), so the containers measured in millilitres are smaller than \(1\text{ L}\).
Order the millilitre containers first: \(100\text{ mL}\) (medicine bottle) then \(250\text{ mL}\) (chocolate milk).
Order the litre containers from smallest to largest: \(1\text{ L}\) (milk), \(2\text{ L}\) (cordial), and \(4\text{ L}\) (fruit juice cask).
Combine the full ordered list from smallest to largest: \(100\text{ mL},\; 250\text{ mL},\; 1\text{ L},\; 2\text{ L},\; 4\text{ L}\).

meta.source: Maths Plus 3 (Stage 2) Student Book · Unit 7: Informal capacity
